content:
This is actually bigger than most realize...

Hermes can now use X like a real tool.

Your AI agent can now search posts, read bookmarks, pull mentions, draft replies, research accounts, manage lists, send DMs, and publish from your account.

So X becomes less like an app you open and more like a data layer your agent can work through.

A few workflows this unlocks:

1. Hermes can search X directly.

This is useful because X is where a lot of useful signal lands first.

Complaints, memes, product launches, narratives, people talking about a market.

You can ask Hermes to search a topic, find what people are saying, summarize the strongest posts, pull out repeated language, or turn it into research.

Probably the most obvious use case.

It's also only the beginning.

2. Hermes can pull your bookmarks.

Bookmarks are no longer a graveyard.

Bookmarks are basically your taste, interests, research, and future ideas trapped inside X.

Now Hermes can turn them into something actually useful.

A weekly digest, an Obsidian vault, a swipe file, a source library for future posts.

The important part is that saved posts finally become memory you can actually use.

3. Hermes can publish posts directly.

This removes the weird gap between having a post ready and actually getting it live.

No scheduler, no copying drafts between tools, no API wiring.

You write it where you already work with Hermes, and it goes up.

The final step is no longer manual.

4. Replies, quotes, and mentions

Hermes can read your mentions, reply, and quote posts.

Mentions/replies on X are honestly almost unusable right now.

Bot accounts, AI slop replies, engagement farmers, accounts tagging everyone just hoping for visibility. The signal-to-noise is brutal.

Hermes can read through all of it and only surface what actually matters.

Especially useful if you post a lot and/or run an account that gets more interaction than you can manually process.

5. Hermes can read timelines and work with lists.

So y

content:
“Bro just send us a quick product video.”

That single sentence had me stuck for almost 2 months.

I’m a Windows creator.

So every brand collab turned into the same painful cycle:

record → re-record → fix audio → edit pauses → sync zooms → export → hate the result → start again

Meanwhile Mac creators were dropping those insanely polished Screen Studio-style videos in 20 minutes.

I genuinely thought: “Okay… maybe Windows just can’t do this properly.”

Then I found Velo

And no exaggeration…

I finished the entire branded product walkthrough in under 30 minutes.

Not just “done”.

Actually polished.

Smooth camera movement. Clean pacing. Natural voice. Professional-looking output. The kind of video that makes brands think you hired an editor.

The crazy part?

The raw recording I gave it was BAD.

I messed up lines. Paused randomly. Clicked the wrong things. Sounded low energy.

Velo basically rebuilt the whole thing into something watchable.

And the brand ended up giving me a bonus because the final video looked THAT good.

That was the moment I realized this isn’t another “AI video tool”.

This is probably the first tool I’ve used that actually understands how creators work.

You don’t need perfect takes anymore.

You just need your thoughts.

Everything else: the cleanup, the pacing, the narration flow, the structure, the presentation—

it handles for you.

Honestly feels like someone took the “Mac creator quality gap” and deleted it for Windows users overnight.

And this is bigger than creators too.

Founders can make launch demos. Teams can make tutorials. Agencies can make client walkthroughs. Educators can make polished lessons. Creators can finally stop wasting 4 hours fixing a 5-minute video.

The most dangerous products are the ones that remove friction you got used to tolerating.

Velo did exactly that.

content:
I never bought the voice AI hype. 

To me they all sounded the same, choppy, robotic, lost the second anyone went off script. 

Every demo I'd ever seen had the same pattern. The agent handled "what are your hours" fine. Then a customer would ask something slightly off-script and it would collapse, repeat itself, talk over them. 

I figured the tech wasn't ready yet. 

Then on this Monday I came across PolyAI. 

They'd just launched their platform and claimed "you can set up the agent in less than 10 mins and it sounds so human that people asked it out on dates." 

I decided to actually try it. 

The setup actually took less than 10 minutes. All I had to do was to share my website URL. 

But after that I decided to take one step further and customise it by telling it what my business does, what kinds of calls usually come in, what to do with the routine ones, and when to flag me. 

It generated the agent. I made a few test calls, tweaked the tone, picked a voice that didn't sound robotic. Done. 

Then I did the part I was actually nervous about. 

I forwarded my business number to it for 24 hours straight with real customers, complex problems and no backup to fall back on. 

I left it alone and went about my day. 

When I sat down with the call log, every single call had been picked up. 

The routine ones about hours, pricing, and directions were handled cleanly without me. Nothing dropped. Nothing missed. 

What actually changed my mind was the voice. It paused. When a caller interrupted, it stopped talking. 

One call ran 9 minutes on a complicated billing question. It solved the issue. 

After my little experiment, here's what I think about Voice AI. 

I dismissed it two years ago because of the gap in usability. The gap between "demo that fails" and "agent that actually works" has closed. 

If you run a business with a phone line, it's worth 10 minutes to see what this looks like for you.

title: The Download: online safety’s future and climate tech’s big pivot
content: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Tech researchers are suing the Trump administration over the future of online safety For months, the Trump administration has been going after researchers who study and try to counter hate speech, harassment, propaganda, and disinformation online. Now, some of those researchers are fighting back.  In a new lawsuit, they’re seeking to strike down a visa restriction policy against “foreign officials and other persons” announced last year by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. They say the policy violates the speech and due process rights of foreign-born workers whose “work supports greater moderation of content on the [tech] platforms.” Find out how the case could impact online safety and free speech . —Eileen Guo Climate tech companies are pivoting to critical minerals We’re over a year into the second Trump administration, and support for climate causes in the US is weak. But climate tech companies are finding ways to survive and even thrive in this new environment, including by looking beyond decarbonization. One example is Boston Metal. The startup has raised a $75 million round to produce critical metals, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report. The company is best known for its efforts to clean up steel production, an industry that’s responsible for about 8% of global greenhouse gas emissions. But the new focus and fresh funds could help it survive a period of waning support for industrial decarbonization. Read the full story on its high-stakes shift . title: Climate tech companies are pivoting to critical minerals
content: We’re over a year into the second Trump administration here in the US, and support for climate causes is weak. But climate tech companies are finding ways to survive and even thrive in this new environment, including by focusing on potential benefits outside decarbonization. Suddenly, it feels like every climate tech company has a story to tell about topics that are politically in vogue: data centers, energy abundance, or critical minerals. In my newest story , I covered Boston Metal’s latest funding round. Largely known for its efforts to produce steel with lower greenhouse gas emissions, the company raised $75 million from new and existing investors to help support its critical metals business. Focusing on metals like niobium and tantalum won’t have the massive climate benefit that cleaner steel would, but it could generate the cash the company needs to keep going. It’s a strategy I’m noticing more as these tough industries like steel look ever tougher to succeed in with limited federal support in the US.   Boston Metal’s molten oxide electrolysis technology uses electricity to produce metals. I covered the startup last year , when it announced a major milestone for its steel business, running its pilot reactor in Massachusetts and producing a literal ton of material. Now the company’s focus has shifted, and it is going all-in on making other metals, from niobium and tantalum (used in aircraft engines and high-end steel alloys) to chromium and vanadium. The steel industry is a difficult one: It operates at a massive scale, and the product doesn’t command too high a price. Focusing on other metals, especially ones the US government deems critical, could be a way to stay afloat, maybe even long enough to meaningfully cut emissions from the steel industry.  “By deploying in the critical metals industry where we can go very fast, we generate the resources to continue with the development of steel,” says Tadeu Carneiro, CEO of Boston Metal. title: Tech researchers are suing the Trump administration over the future of online safety
content: Since its earliest days back in office, the Trump administration has been going after researchers who study and try to counter hate speech, harassment, propaganda, and disinformation online.  Now, some of those researchers are fighting back. Last week their lawsuit—which could have global repercussions for online safety and free speech—made its first appearance in court .  This fight started a year ago, when US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced on X what he called a “visa restriction policy” against “foreign officials and other persons” who were “complicit in censoring Americans.” Since then, a handful of foreign officials and researchers have been barred from travel to the US, and in theory, anyone working in fact-checking or online trust and safety more broadly could face the same restrictions.  Still, the exact implications of Rubio’s announcement are unclear—purposefully so, argues Carrie DeCell, a lawyer representing the researchers. “This policy is expansive and incredibly vague, and the chilling effects are correspondingly enormous,” DeCell said outside the courthouse in Washington, DC, on May 13.   The case has been brought by the Coalition for Independent Technology Research (CITR), an advocacy organization for tech researchers. It is suing Rubio, former US secretary of homeland security Kristi Noem, and former US attorney general Pam Bondi and asking the court to strike down the policy as unconstitutional. In their complaint, the plaintiffs say the policy violates the speech and due process rights of foreign-born tech researchers and workers whose “work supports greater moderation of content on the [tech] platforms.” CITR is represented by Columbia University’s Knight First Amendment Institute and the legal nonprofit Protect Democracy. DeCell, a senior staff attorney at the Knight Institute, tells MIT Technology Review that they’re in court because the Trump administration is effectively “using immigration law to punis

title: Musk v. Altman: Much ado about nothing
content: Today I’m talking with Liz Lopatto, who spent the last month covering the Musk v. Altman trial in all its chaos. You’ll hear her describe the courthouse as a “zoo” and explain that there were protests of one kind or another happening outside every day. Both Elon Musk and Sam Altman are big personalities, and people have a lot of feelings about both of them and the AI industry. And in the end… nothing happened! The jury found that Elon had filed his lawsuit after the statute of limitations had run out. You’ll hear Liz explain exactly what’s going on there. Beyond that, the trial was nominally about OpenAI’s conversion to a for-profit entity from a nonprofit one and if the way OpenAI went about it cost Elon Musk money. But really, the suit seems mostly to have been about Elon Musk being mad at Sam Altman — or at OpenAI, for being successful without him — and wanting him punished in some way. So in a room full of untrustworthy, unreliable people all fighting with each other, did anyone even have a reputation left to lose? Is there a floor? Okay: Liz Lopatto on Musk v. Altman . Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Liz Lopatto, you are a senior chaos reporter here at The Verge . You just covered the Sam Altman v. Elon Musk trial. 今回使ったプロンプトはこちら

✅️使い方

①下記のプロンプト一番上の
「n=◯」を、一括作成したい枚数に変更してください（10枚上限）

②【テイスト】【ランダム化する要素】を自由に変更してください

③難しい方は、下のプロンプトをそのままChatGPTにコピペして一緒に編集してもらえばOK！

=======
n=5

以下の条件で、画像をn枚生成してください。

各画像ごとに、指定したランダム要素からそれぞれ1つずつ選び、組み合わせてください。

【目的】
ランダム性が視覚的に分かりやすい画像を作りたいです。
n枚を並べたときに、見た瞬間に違いが分かるようにしてください。
単なる微差ではなく、選ばれた要素の違いがはっきり伝わるようにしてください。

【重要ルール】
- n枚すべて別案として成立させること
- できるだけ同じ候補を繰り返さないこと
- 各画像の違いが一目で分かるように、ランダム要素を強く反映すること
- 選ばれた候補一覧や説明文は画像内に表示しないこと
- 画像内には、選ばれた「文字の内容」だけを大きく表示すること
- 背景は白または透過風でシンプルにすること
- キャラクターを大きく、はっきり、親しみやすく描くこと
- 文字は極太で大きく、スマホでも読みやすく表示すること
- 既存キャラクターに似せず、完全オリジナルで作成すること

【テイスト】
- ゆるくて可愛い
- LINEスタンプ風
- 輪郭は太め
- スマホ画面でも見やすい
- 表情は大げさで分かりやすい

content:
Most people use Claude Code like autocomplete.

But Claude Code is actually a full agent operating system.

And most engineers are only using Layer 1.

Here’s the architecture nobody explains properly:

🧠 Layer 1 — CLAUDE.md

This is the agent’s constitution.

Your:
→ architecture rules
→ coding standards
→ repo structure
→ naming conventions
→ workflows

All live here.

Always loaded.
Always active.

This is what turns Claude from “generic AI” into “your engineering team’s AI.”

📚 Layer 2 — Skills

Reusable expertise modules.

Claude dynamically loads the right SKILL.md only when needed.

That means:
→ cleaner context
→ lower token usage
→ specialized execution
→ less hallucination

The important part most people miss:

Skills can fork into isolated subagents.

So your main context stays clean while deep tasks execute separately.

This is where Claude starts feeling agentic instead of conversational.

🛡️ Layer 3 — Hooks

The most underrated layer in the stack.

Hooks are deterministic infrastructure triggers:

→ PreToolUse
→ PostToolUse
→ SessionStart
→ Stop

This is NOT AI reasoning.

It’s programmable guardrails.

Examples:
→ auto-run linting
→ block dangerous bash commands
→ enforce repo policies
→ send Slack notifications
→ auto-format outputs
→ inject runtime context

Production reliability happens here.

Most teams skip this layer completely.

Huge mistake.

🤝 Layer 4 — Subagents

This is where Claude Code becomes a true multi-agent system.

Delegate tasks downward.
Receive results upward.

Each subagent gets:
→ isolated context
→ separate tools
→ different permissions
→ independent models

No context bleed.
No recursive chaos.
Hard boundaries by design.

You stop thinking:
“One AI assistant”

And start thinking:
“Distributed cognitive workers.”

📦 Layer 5 — Plugins

The distribution layer.

Bundle:
→ skills
→ hooks
→ commands
→ agents
→ workflows

into one installable package.

One command:
Entire team inherits the same behavior instantly.

• All using your existing ChatGPT subscription

You literally get Claude planning + Codex executing in one workflow.

Not a wrapper. Not a hack. Not a community fork.

OpenAI shipped a plugin that connects their agent

Two competing AI labs.
One terminal.
One codebase.

That sentence shouldn’t exist in 2026.

The commands are clean:

/codex:review → full code review
/codex:adversarial-review → challenge architecture decisions
/codex:rescue → hand off bugs to Codex
/codex:status → track background jobs
/codex:result → fetch output

You can literally say:

“Ask Codex to investigate why tests are failing”

…and it runs in the background while you keep coding.

No API keys required.
Works with ChatGPT subscription.
Installs in one command.
100% open source.

This is the first real multi-agent coding workflow inside a single terminal.

@cursor_ai just dropped Composer 2.5 and the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index results are ridiculous. The model scored 62, a 14 point jump from the previous version, securing 3rd place behind Claude Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.5.

This is what the cost-quality frontier looks like in 2026. Huge congrats to the Cursor team.

content:
【生データ全部流します】

5月19日にAIマーケティング構築講座内で開催した
“無限質問回答LIVE”で出たQ&Aを全て公開します。

今AI中級者が抱えている悩みと
それに対する解決策が全てわかるのでガチ有益。

4時間半ぶっ続けで質問回答した内容なので
これ見ればほぼ解決すると思います笑↓

01. Codex / Claude Code / ローカルAI環境
Q：Codexをローカルファイルと紐付けるには？
A：まず自分のMac内にAI用フォルダを作ります。その後、Codexで新規チャットを開き、「新しいプロジェクト追加」からそのフォルダを選択すればOKです。以後、そのフォルダ内でファイル作成、フォルダ整理、スキル改善、ナレッジ更新までできます。
Q：ローカルでAIを使うメリットは？
A：速いことです。ローカルにファイルがあるので読み書きが速く、スキルやナレッジの修正も爆速になります。さらにAPIキーなども安全に管理できれば、外部サービス連携までかなりやりやすくなります。
Q：AI専用フォルダはiCloud Driveでもいい？
A：ローカルに同期されていて、AIが実体ファイルを触れるなら大丈夫です。ただ、クラウド側にしか実体がなく毎回ダウンロードが必要な状態だと不安定です。おすすめはローカルフォルダ、複数PCで使うならSyncthingのような同期です。
Q：Syncthingは何がいい？
A：無料で、複数PC間のフォルダをかなり速く同期できます。メインPCとサブPCに同じAI用フォルダを置けるので、サブPCでオートメーションを回しながら、メインPCでも同じファイルを触れます。
Q：Mac miniやサブPCをAI運用に使う意味は？
A：常時起動しておける端末があると、ルーティンやオートメーションを回しやすいです。メインPCを閉じていても、サブPC側でCodexやClaude Codeを動かせる状態を作れるのが強いです。
Q：外出中はAI作業できない？
A：できます。スマホではリサーチ、壁打ち、プロンプト作成までやっておき、帰宅後にそのプロンプトをCodexやClaude Codeへ投げるのがおすすめです。移動中に設計して、ローカル環境で実行する流れです。
Q：AI用フォルダはどう整理すればいい？
A：経営の組織図をフォルダで作るイメージです。SNS、YouTube、経理、セールス、リストマーケなど、仕事単位で事業部フォルダを作り、その中にスキル、ナレッジ、チェックシート、アカウント情報、進捗を置いていきます。
Q：既存のフォルダがぐちゃぐちゃな場合は？
A：いきなり本番フォルダで整理せず、まずバックアップを取って、そのコピーにディレクトリ構築プロンプトを走らせるのが安全です。良さそうなら本番運用に寄せる、微妙なら構造を調整します。
Q：Claude Codeで作ったスキルはCodexでも使える？
A：同じフォルダを参照できる状態なら、Claude Code用に作ったスキルやナレッジをCodex側でも活用しやすいです。必要に応じて、Codex向けの前提やモデル指定だけスキル内で調整します。画像・スライド系だけCodex前提のフォルダを作る運用もありです。
Q：CodexとClaude Codeはどちらがいい？
A：どちらも強いです。Codexはふわっとした指示でも一旦やりきってくれる印象。Claude Codeは正確に進めるために確認を挟みやすい印象です。ちゃんとスキルとナレッジを作れば、どちらでもかなり安定します。
Q：初心者はCursorを使うべき？
A：最初からCursorにこだわらなくて大丈夫です。今はCodexやClaude Codeのデスクトップアプリでローカルを触れるので、初心者はまずそちらでフォルダを扱う感覚に慣れるのがおすすめです。
Q：PCのスペックはどれくらい必要？
A：16GBあればかなり安心ですが、8GBでも使っている人はいます。重い処理は難しいかもしれませんが、CodexやClaude Codeの導入自体は多くのPCで可能です。

02. スライド / 画像生成 / デザイン
Q：Image2でスライドはどこまで作れる？
A：かなりいけます。台本、スライド作成スキル、参考デザインを渡せば、ノー編集に近いレベルのスライドも出せます。Googleスライドへのアップロードやリンク共有も、API連携しておけば効率化できます。
Q：スライド作成スキルはどうカスタマイズする？
A：スキルフォルダ内のリファレンス画像やPDFを、自分が作りたいデザインに差し替えます。過去資料、真似したい資料、トンマナが近い画像を入れて、テスト出力しながら改善します。
Q：参考画像を入れ替えるだけで十分？
A：画像を入れ替

title:
Andrej Karpathy just explained the future of software engineering without directly saying it.

The best AI engineers are no longer “prompting.”

They’re building systems around the agents.

Karpathy’s
content:
Andrej Karpathy just explained the future of software engineering without directly saying it.

The best AI engineers are no longer “prompting.”

They’re building systems around the agents.

Karpathy’s biggest insight wasn’t:
“Claude can code.”

It was:
LLMs become dramatically better when you force them into disciplined workflows.

That’s why "CLAUDE.md" files are suddenly everywhere.

Not because they’re prompts.

Because they behave like an operating system for the agent.

Karpathy called out the exact problems with AI coding:

- models assume instead of asking
- they overengineer simple tasks
- they hide confusion
- they rewrite unrelated code
- they optimize for completion, not correctness

So developers started encoding rules directly into the workflow:

→ Think before coding
→ Simplicity first
→ Surgical edits only
→ Goal-driven execution

And the results are wild.

People are now running multiple Claude Code agents in parallel like engineering teams:

• one agent researching
• one debugging
• one writing tests
• one optimizing code
• one validating outputs

Not “AI assistance.”

Actual orchestration.

And this part from Karpathy changes everything:

“Don’t tell the model what to do. Give it success criteria and let it loop.”

That is the shift.

From:
“write this function”

To:
“here’s the goal, constraints, tests, and verification system — now iterate until correct.”

The craziest part?

This already feels like a phase shift in engineering.

A lot of developers quietly went from:
80% manual coding → to 80% agent-driven coding in just months.

Not because AI became perfect.

Because the leverage became impossible to ignore.

We’re entering an era where the highest leverage engineers won’t necessarily be the best coders.

They’ll be the people who build the best systems around AI agents.

content:
AI coding agents just crossed an important line most developers haven’t noticed yet.

Claude Code quietly replaced "/simplify" with "/code-review".

But the real shift is the new “effort” system.

You can now decide exactly how much reasoning the model should use before touching your code:
• low → instant lightweight tasks
• medium → cheaper token-efficient workflows
• high → balanced reasoning for serious development
• xhigh → optimized for advanced coding + agentic work
• max → deepest reasoning mode for complex engineering problems

And the crazy part?

This is the first time AI coding feels truly compute-native.

We’re no longer just prompting models…
we’re allocating intelligence, reasoning depth, and inference budget like engineering infrastructure.

AI assistants are evolving into programmable software engineers.

content:
10 GitHub repos so good they shouldn't be free.

1. AutoHedge

An autonomous hedge fund built in Python with four AI agents: a director generates investment theses, a quant validates them, a risk manager decides position size, and an execution agent places orders. Operates live on Solana. With 'pip install -U autohedge', you can start trading immediately.
repo → https://t.co/YTc8jHhRLo

2. Vibe-Trading

A trading system using a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) model, featuring 64 finance skills and 29 preset specialist agent swarms. Includes analysis methods like Ichimoku, Elliott Wave, SMC, Black-Scholes, full Greeks, and risk parity. Its crypto desk provides liquidation heatmaps and token unlock tracking. You can observe agents debating strategies in real time.
repo → https://t.co/LcBLbWMcAk

3. Fincept Terminal

A Bloomberg Terminal replacement that runs on your laptop. CFA levels 1, 2, and 3 analytics. 20+ investor AI agents (Buffett, Dalio, Soros). 100+ data connectors, including Polygon, World Bank, and IMF. Bloomberg charges $24,000 a year. This is free.
repo → https://t.co/5D3m8P5Sfu

4. LibreChat

Every model ChatGPT runs, plus Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, and 20 more. Self-hosted. Native MCP support. You own the data, the history, the infrastructure. OpenAI charges $20/month to use their wrapper. This costs nothing to use your own.
repo → https://t.co/h5Wn1OIJzR

5. Open Higgsfield AI

A self-hosted cinema studio with 200+ AI models. Flux, Midjourney, Sora, Kling, Veo, GPT-4o, SDXL all in one interface. Text to image. Image to video. Cinema mode with pro camera controls. No subscription. Your data stays local.
repo → https://t.co/iQwE8LmB9N

6. Open-LLM-VTuber

A Live2D AI companion that runs offline, sees your screen, hears your voice, and never forgets. Inner thoughts are shown as a separate text layer, so you watch the reasoning happen before words come out. Pet mode floats it on your desktop. Swap the LLM in one config line.
repo → https://t.co/JcFPhFt69G

content:
Your AI coding bill should not be a mystery

AI Token Monitor is a macOS and Windows system tray app for tracking Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode token usage, cost, and activity in real time.

It helps you see where your coding-agent budget is going by parsing local session JSONL files, showing charts and model breakdowns, and adding alerts when usage crosses thresholds.

Key features:

• Real-time token tracking – parses Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode session files for live usage stats
• Cost + activity views – shows today’s usage, 7/30-day charts, weekly/monthly totals, and activity heatmaps
• Multi-account directories – aggregate work and personal Claude/Codex roots in one dashboard
• Alerts + webhooks – tray cost display plus Discord, Slack, and Telegram notifications for thresholds/resets
• Opt-in social layer – leaderboard, badges, chat, and monthly/yearly AI Report without sharing code or conversation content

It’s open-source (MIT license).

title: Anthropic’s Code with Claude showed off coding’s future—whether you like it or not
content: The vibes were strong at Code with Claude, Anthropic’s two-day event for software developers in London that kicked off on May 19, the same day as Google’s I/O in Palo Alto. (A coincidence, not a flex, Anthropic staffers assured me.) “Who here has shipped a pull request in the last week that was completely written by Claude?” Jeremy Hadfield, an engineer at Anthropic, asked from the main stage. Almost half the people in the packed room—many sitting with laptops on their knees, coding or prompting as they watched the talks—raised their hands. Pull requests are fixes or updates to existing software that are submitted for review before they go live. They are the bread and butter of software development, the chunks of code that most professional developers spend their lives writing—or did until now. “Who here has shipped a pull request that was completely written by Claude where they did not read the code at all?” Hadfield asked next. Nervous laughter. Most of the hands stayed up. It’s not news that LLM-powered tools like Anthropic’s Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex have upended the way software gets made. Top tech companies now like to boast of how little code their developers write by hand. (“Most software at Anthropic is now written by Claude,” Hadfield said. “Claude has written most of the code in Claude Code.”) OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft make similar claims. Many others wish they could. Even so, it is striking how normal this new paradigm already seems, and how fast it has set in. This was the second year that Anthropic has put on developer events, which also run in San Francisco and Tokyo. This time last year, the company had just released Claude 4. It could code, kind of. But with Anthropic’s latest string of updates—especially Claude 4.6 and then 4.7, released in February and April—Claude Code is a tool that more and more developers seem happy to hand their work off to. Let Claude cook. ANTHROPIC (GRAPHIC) / WILL DOUGLAS HEAVEN (PHOTO) Anthropic says its goal is

title: Outlookで画像が表示されない不具合が再発　Microsoftが原因を調査中
content: Microsoftが 新しいサポートドキュメント を公開し、Outlookの基本機能のひとつである「メール内の画像表示」に問題が発生していることを正式に認めました。メール本文やニュースレター、署名に挿入した画像が正しく表示されず、赤い×印やエラーが出るケースがあるとのことです。 この不具合はVersion 2604 Build 19929.20164以降で発生しており、以下のメッセージが表示される場合があるとのことです(されない場合もある)。 The linked image cannot be displayed. The file may have been moved, renamed, or deleted. Verify that the link points to the correct file and location. リンクされている画像を表示できません。ファイルが移動、名前の変更、または削除された可能性があります。リンク先が正しいファイルと場所を指しているか確認してください。 原因のひとつとして、メール内で画像を扱う際に使われるContent-ID(cid)が正しく処理されず、XMLタグとして埋め込まれるべき情報が壊れている可能性が示されています。 Outlookでは過去にもQuick Stepsの長期的な不具合が発生しており、今回も「基本機能が壊れる系」のトラブルとして注目されています。 Microsoftが案内している確認方法 Microsoft は、この不具合に該当しているかどうかを確認するために、クラシック版 Outlook で メールのソースを直接チェックする方法 を案内しています。 クラシックOutlookでメールを開く リボンからMove → Actions → Other Actions → View Sourceを選択 ソース内でcidを検索し、次の 2 つのタグがセットで存在するか確認する <v:imagedata src="cid:image001.png@01DCE6B1.CF669A40" o:title="" /> <w:wrap type="topAndBottom"/> cid画像+ wrap=TopAndBottomの組み合わせがあり、画像が表示されていない場合、この問題が発生している可能性があります。 暫定的な回避策 Microsoftは調査を進めているものの、現時点では根本的な修正は提供されていません。そのため、暫定的な回避策として 「Wrap Text(折り返し)でTop and Bottomを使わない」 ことを推奨しています。 これは、今回の不具合がcid画像× wrap=TopAndBottomの組み合わせで発生するためだと思われます。 完全な解決にはアップデートが必要になる見込みで、続報が待たれます。

title: MicrosoftのOOXMLは「標準」ではない──TDFが示すデジタル主権の条件
content: LibreOfficeを開発するThe Document Foundation(TDF)が、Microsoft Officeの文書形式「OOXML」やExcelの日付処理について 強い批判 を行っています。 TDFはこれまでもMicrosoftの独自仕様に対して問題提起を続けてきましたが、今回のブログ投稿ではその姿勢をさらに鮮明にしています。 ODFとOOXMLの根本的な違い TDFが強調するのは、LibreOfficeが採用するODF(OpenDocument Format)が「真にオープン」であり、特定ベンダーに支配されないということです。 MicrosoftのOOXMLは「オープンと名乗っているだけ」で、実際にはMicrosoftが独占的にコントロールしているとし、仕様書は7,500ページ以上に及び、透明性や標準化の観点からも問題が多いとしています。 OOXML：Microsoft Office が標準で使っている文書形式。 ODF：独立した標準団体が管理するオープン形式。 Excelの日付処理は「最悪レベル」？ TDFはまた、Excelの日付処理を強く批判しています。1900年を誤って閏年として扱うなど、歴史的に知られた問題がいまだに残っており、「日付を間違えるソフトは他にもあるが、Excelほどひどいものはない」とまで述べています。 この問題が現実に影響した例として、2020年に遺伝子名がExcelによって勝手に日付へ変換される事態が続き、研究者が数十の遺伝子名を変更せざるを得なかったケースが紹介されています。 人間の遺伝子にはSEPT1やMARCH1のように、月名(Sep、Mar)＋数字という形式のものが多数存在しますが、Excelはこれを見て、SEPT1 → 1-Sep(9月1日)、MARCH1 → 1-Mar(3月1日)のように自動で日付に変換してしまったそうです。 真のデジタル主権とは何か TDFは、OOXMLが世界的に普及した理由について「MicrosoftがISOや政治家を巻き込み、OOXMLを移行用の一時的な形式だと説明したため」と主張。実際には、2010年以降もOOXMLはstrict仕様へ移行せず、現在に至るまでMicrosoftが独占的に扱う形式のままだと批判しています。 TDFは、(Officeソフトが)ODFをサポートするだけでは不十分で、標準形式としてネイティブに採用しなければデジタル主権は確立できないと結論づけています。そして、互換性のために使われるべきはOOXMLではなく、むしろOOXMLを交換用フォーマットとして扱うべきだと主張しています。

title: iOS 27対応機種に大きな変化、iPhone 11世代が対象外になる可能性
content: Appleが6月8日のWWDCで発表予定のiOS 27について、対応機種に大きな変更があるというリーク情報が話題になっています。今回の噂が正しければ、これまでiOS 26を利用できていた4つのモデルがリストから外れる可能性があります。 iPhone 11世代が対象外に？ 先月、中国のSNS、WeiboにリーカーInstant Digitalが投稿した「 iOS 27対応モデル一覧 」には、以下の4機種が含まれていません。 iPhone 11 Pro Max iPhone 11 Pro iPhone 11 iPhone SE(第2世代) 投稿によると、iOS 27はiPhone 12以降が必須とされており、SEシリーズも第3世代以降のみが対象になるとのことです。 2年連続での大幅な切り捨てになる可能性 もしこの情報が正しければ、Appleは昨年のiPhone XS世代に続き、2年連続で複数モデルをメジャーアップデート対象から外すことになります。ただし、サポート外になったとしてもiOS 26のセキュリティアップデートは継続されるため、すぐに使えなくなるわけではありません。 なお、iOS 27では、以下のような大きな変更が期待されています。 Siriの大幅刷新 「Liquid Glass」のアップデート Apple Intelligence(AI機能)の強化 特に Apple Intelligence は iPhone 15 Pro 以降が必須とされており、たとえ iOS 27 にアップデートできても、すべての新機能を利用できるわけではない点がポイントです。 まとめ: iPhone 11世代はついに役目を終えるのか iPhone 11シリーズは、iPhone 6s世代と並ぶほど長期間アップデートを受けてきたモデルです。今回の噂が事実なら、ついにその役目を終えるタイミングが来たとも言えます。正式な対応モデルは WWDC で明らかになるため、ユーザーとしては発表を待つしかありません。 [via 9to5Mac ]

title: Scaling creativity in the age of AI
content: Storytelling is core to humanity’s DNA, stemming from our impulse to express ideals, warnings, hopes, and experiences. Technology has always been woven through the medium and the distribution: from early humans’ innovation of natural pigments and charcoals for cave paintings to literal representation by the camera. The landscape of storytelling continues to shift under our feet. Social and streaming platforms have multiplied, audiences have fragmented, and our demand for fresh, unique media is insatiable. A recent McKinsey podcast cites that we are watching upwards of 12 hours of video content daily, often on multiple devices and multiple platforms. All this content is expensive to produce: With a baseline budget of $150M, a Hollywood feature runs $1M per minute of finished film; prestige streaming content is in the hundreds of thousands per minute. And since consumers want to engage with authentic, original material , every company is now effectively a media company. That means we all face the same pressure: more content, with the same time and budget constraints. There is no longer a question whether to use AI for content; the math doesn’t work any other way. What leaders need to focus on now is how to adapt responsibly, protect brand integrity, uplift team creativity, and build customer trust. A few things worth holding onto as this era accelerates: AI amplifies what’s already there, both good and bad. Weak strategy stays weak. Responsible adoption means knowing what’s in your tools and models. Provenance and transparency are the foundation, not the finish line. Scale without taste is just noise. Investing in your team’s judgment is what makes more content matter. Fundamentals of great storytelling have not changed. Regardless of format or channel, what makes audiences lean in are still characters, arc, ingenuity, and surprise. content:
「ChatGPT in PowerPoint」公開
ついに来た！これが欲しかった。
「画像生成してスライドに入れて」ができる！
しかもレイアウト調整も勝手にやってくれる。

🎨パワポの画像生成から配置まで自動化
「ChatGPT in PowerPoint」を活用し、スライドの表紙に合う画像を自動生成して配置する機能を検証しました。テキストだけのシンプルな表紙から、指示を出すだけでおにぎりの画像を生成し、瞬時に洗練されたレイアウトへと仕上げてくれます。

💡 修正指示もチャットで完結
自動生成された画像に対して、追加の要望をチャットで伝えるだけで修正が可能です。動画内ではおにぎりの海苔の巻き方に違和感があったため「一番手前のおにぎりの海苔がおかしいから直して」と指示したところ、違和感のない綺麗な画像へスムーズに差し替えてくれました。

🎨 スライド作成の未来が変わる
画像生成から配置、さらにはその後の細かい修正までをすべてチャット上のやり取りだけで完結できるのが魅力です。デザインの知識がなくても、AIと対話しながら直感的にクオリティの高いスライドを作成できるため、資料作成の効率が劇的に向上します。

content:
The AI-native marketing team has 4 levels:

LEVEL 1: AI assistant

You → ChatGPT / Claude

This is where most teams start. They use AI for drafts, summaries, research, email, and meeting notes.

Useful, but still person-by-person.

----

LEVEL 2: role-tuned agents

Content agent  
SEO agent  
Paid media agent  
Outbound agent  
Sales-call agent  
Creative agent  

Each agent has a job, context, and output standard.

The team stops asking “what can AI do?” and starts asking “which workflow should this agent own?”

----

LEVEL 3: company brain

The agents stop working from isolated prompts.

They pull from shared context:

Gong calls  
ICP notes  
Past winners  
Brand rules  
Client patterns  
SOPs  
Objections  
Offers  
Case studies  

This is where AI starts compounding.

One agent learns something, and every other agent can use it.

----

LEVEL 4: closed-loop revenue system

This is where it gets interesting.

Sales calls create content angles.  
Content creates leads.  
Leads feed outbound.  
Outbound replies update the ICP.  
The ICP updates the company brain.  
The company brain improves the agents.

The marketing team stops being a group of task owners.

It becomes an operating system.

content:
Hermes Agentの理論を
大解剖した海外投稿が話題。

Hermes Agentは先日より
X Premiumのサブスク対応でも
トレンドとなっていますよね。

このHermes Agentが
具体的にどのような仕組みで動いているのか
日本語で整理しました↓

1. Hermes Agentとは実際に何なのか

一言で表すと、使えば使うほど良くなるAIエージェント。

従来の多くのAIエージェントは、セッションが終わるとユーザーの好みやプロジェクトのルールなど、文脈を忘れてしまいます。

Hermes Agentはこの問題に対して、以下の3つを組み合わせています。

1) 実行時のスキル学習
作業中に得た成功パターンを、再利用可能なスキルとして保存する。
2) 永続的な多層メモリ
ユーザー情報、プロジェクト情報、過去会話などを複数レイヤーで保持する。
3) GEPAによるオフライン最適化
実行ログをもとに、スキルを後から検証・改善する。

この3つによって、Hermes Agentは経験を蓄積していくAIエージェントになっています。

2. OpenClawとの違い

Hermes Agentは、学習するAIエージェントそのものを中心に作られています。つまり、「どう記憶するか」「どう作業手順を覚えるか」「どう改善していくか」が主役です。

一方でOpenClawは、メッセージングや外部とのやり取りを中心に作られているイメージです。つまり、Telegramやチャットのような入口を通じて、エージェントとやり取りしやすくすることに強みがあります。

したがって、どちらが優れているというより、設計思想が違うのです。

3. どのように構築されているのか

Hermes Agentの中核は、「run_agent.py」内のAIAgentクラスです。

CLI、メッセージング、バッチ処理、IDE連携など、使い方はいくつかあります。しかし、どの入口から使うとしても、最終的には同じ中核エージェントにつながります。

窓口は複数あるが、中で働いているエージェントは同じ、と考えると分かりやすいかもしれません。

そして、基本的な処理ループはReActスタイルの同期型ループです。流れとしては、以下のようになります。

1) システムプロンプトを構築する
2) コンテキスト圧縮が必要か確認する
3) API呼び出しを行う
4) ツール呼び出しがあれば実行する
5) 必要に応じて再びループする

さらに、Hermes Agentは実行場所も柔軟に変えることが可能。それは、たとえばローカルターミナルやDocker、SSHなど。

設定を変えるだけで、ローカルPCからクラウドGPUサーバーなどへ実行環境を移せる設計ということです。

また、使うAIモデルも固定されていません。Claude、GPT、Gemini、Ollamaなどに対応できるように、モデルごとの差を吸収する仕組みがあります。

他にも、Hermes Agentには1タスクあたり「90ターン」の上限があります。これは、エージェントが失敗した処理を何度も繰り返して、気づかないうちにAPI利用料を消費し続けることを防ぐためです。

4. エージェントとは何者なのか

Hermes Agentでは、メモリやスキルの前に、まずエージェントの人格を定義します。そこで「SOUL.md」が使われます。

これは、エージェントにとっての「基本人格」や「仕事の姿勢」を決めるファイルです。たとえば、「どのような立場で振る舞うのか」「どんな口調で返すのか」「何を優先して判断するのか」といった内容を定義します。

ここで重要となるのは、Hermes Agentでは以下のように役割が明確に分かれているということ。

・SOUL.md: エージェントの人格
・Memory: エージェントが覚えていること
・Skills: エージェントが実行できる作業手順

通常、メモリやスキルが増えても、エージェントの基本姿勢が毎回変わると一貫性がなくなります。そのため、SOUL.mdが土台となり、その上にメモリやスキルが積み上がっていく構造になっているのです。

5. メモリシステム

Hermes Agentのメモリは、1つの大きな記憶領域ではなく、用途に応じて3つの層に分かれています。

Tier 1: 常に使う小さなメモリ

まず中核になるのが、「MEMORY.md」と「USER.md」。

MEMORY.md: プロジェクトのルール、ツールの癖、過去に学んだ教訓などを保存。
USER.md: ユーザーの名前、コミュニケーションの好み、スキルレベル、避けるべき表現などを保存。

この2つはセッション開始時に読み込まれるため

He pastes any ad or sales page in, they critique it, the
content:
This guy made $260K off one AI agent workflow. 

The whole thing runs on a virtual focus group of 13 AI personas trained to be his customers. 

He pastes any ad or sales page in, they critique it, the system rewrites it, and a prediction engine picks the winner before he spends a dollar on traffic. 

@IMJustinBrooke came on the pod to walk us through it.

Here's what I learned:

1) He built a virtual focus group. 13 AI personas critique your ad in parallel, a copywriter agent rewrites it three ways, a prediction engine picks the winner. 13 cents per run.

2) The accuracy is academically validated. Harvard, Stanford, and the NYT have published studies on this. NYT clocked it at 92% accuracy versus human focus groups.

3) Multiple personas beat one ICP. Every copy book preaches one persona. The math says otherwise. Same room of buyers has men, women, young, old, local, software. The mix is the point.

4) The personas are not prompts. They're 1,400 word dossiers with demographics, pain points, empathy maps, and decision making process. Skip the dossier work and you get garbage.

5) Wash everything before it ships. Every ad, sales page, LinkedIn post, tweet. A top 1% copywriter charges $500 an ad. This is 13 cents.

6) "Embody" beats "pretend" as a prompt verb. Machines hear "pretend" as fake-be-this-thing. They hear "embody" as become it.

7) The copywriter agent formats output like an internal team email. Quoted feedback, brief insights, three rewrites. Way more useful than the default AI report format.

8) Each persona votes yes or no on buying. His Black Friday offer scored 7 yeses out of 13. Did $36,000 in revenue. The nos were the wrong-fit personas anyway.

9) It doubles as a copywriting school. The rewrites sometimes contain bullets better than yours and you just steal them. Justin has 20 years in direct response and openly admits the AI catches him slipping.

10) Where to start: build the personas first. Take a weekend, use Claude deep research, write 5 to 13 r

title:
How do AI Coding Agents understand a million-line codebase? Let's understand.

A coding agent like Claude Code or Cursor cannot read the entire codebase at once. The context window is limited. Even a
content:
How do AI Coding Agents understand a million-line codebase? Let's understand.

A coding agent like Claude Code or Cursor cannot read the entire codebase at once. The context window is limited. Even a medium-sized repository will not fit.

So, how does it work?

The agent does not load everything. It explores selectively, just like a human developer.

Let's say we ask the agent to fix a bug in the login flow.

First, it looks at the directory structure to understand the project.

Then, it uses grep to find files that mention login or auth.

After that, it reads only the relevant files - not the whole codebase.

This is called agentic exploration. The agent uses tools to navigate the codebase step by step.

Few important tools the agent uses:
- List files - to see the project structure
- Grep or search - to find symbols and keywords
- Read a file - to load it into context
- Follow imports - to jump from one file to another

Many agents also read project files like README first. These give a quick overview of the project before deeper exploration.

Some agents go one step further and use embeddings. The codebase is chunked and converted into vectors. When we ask a question, the agent finds the most relevant chunks using semantic search.

The agent builds a working mental model from these small pieces. It does not need to see everything. It only needs to see what is relevant to our task.

This is how AI Coding Agents understand a large codebase - by exploring selectively.

content:
How it works under the hood

The flow has four stages:

1. Generate. When you submit a prompt, the frontend opens a Server-Sent Events connection to POST /api/autogit/generate.
The API server forwards your prompt to whichever AI provider you chose (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, DeepSeek, or Groq) using your own API key the key never touches our database, it stays in your browser. The model returns a structured JSON payload containing all the files for your project. We parse and validate that payload, then persist the session to PostgreSQL so nothing is lost if you refresh.

2. Edit. The editor loads your generated files with syntax highlighting and a live preview iframe that renders the HTML in a sandboxed environment. A chat panel lets you iterate describe what you want to change and the AI rewrites the relevant files in-place. Every iteration goes through POST /api/autogit/improve, which streams updates back the same way the initial generation does.

3. Deploy. When you click Deploy, POST /api/autogit/deploy takes over. Using a GitHub App installation token, the backend creates a new repository under your GitHub account, pushes all the project files in a single commit, and enables GitHub Pages. A GitHub Actions workflow handles the Vite build and publishes the output. Your app is live at https://t.co/gJLWsHY3b6 within a couple of minutes no CLI, no local git, no manual config.

4. Push updates. After the initial deploy, every subsequent save goes through POST /api/autogit/push. Rather than re-cloning the repo, we fetch the current SHA for each file via the GitHub Contents API, then issue a PUT request per file. GitHub Actions picks up the commit and redeploys automatically.

Why this architecture

We kept the API key client-side intentionally. It means zero credential storage on our end and zero risk of a server-side leak. The SSE streaming model keeps the UI responsive during generation you see status events in real time rather than staring at a spinner. The SHA-bas

title: AIに話しかけるための音声入力は、無料OSSでもかなりいけるかもしれない
content: 最近、AIに指示を出すときの入力方法をかなり見直していました。 結論から言うと、Whispur という無料・オープンソースのmacOS音声入力アプリを自分用に少し調整したら、「AIに話しかけるための音声入力」としては、もう有料アプリなしでもかなり実用的だと感じています。 人間に送る文章をそのまま作る用途なら、まだ有料の音声入力アプリの方が強い場面はあります。誤字の少なさ、文章の整え方、UIの完成度はやはり大事です。 でも、相手がChatGPTやCodexやClaude CodeのようなAIなら、少し事情が変わります。 完璧な文章でなくても、意味がだいたい伝わればAIがかなり補ってくれるか...
author: yosiki

title: As Grok flounders, SpaceX bets future on beating Big Tech at AI
content: Elon Musk’s SpaceX has highlighted AI as the tentpole of the company’s future, projecting a multi-trillion-dollar market opportunity that rivals the total value of all US economic activity. But the company must first win over customers who generally favor AI models from competitors such as OpenAI and Anthropic. SpaceX described its traditional space launch and satellite business as playing a supporting role to its fledgling AI business in financial disclosures that preceded an expected initial public offering of company stock. That stems from SpaceX having formally acquired Musk’s company xAI earlier this year—the SpaceXAI division now oversees the Grok AI models and the associated Grok chatbot previously developed by xAI. The SpaceX S-1 filing claimed that the company has “the largest actionable total addressable market in human history” and highlighted AI as representing most of that opportunity at an estimated $26.5 trillion market—a number that comes close to rivaling US nominal GDP that stood at nearly $32 trillion in the first quarter of 2026.
